entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10121"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 25</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.25.1-Jer.25.38">Jr 25:1-38</reference>. Prophecy of the Seventy Years' Captivity; and after That the Destruction of Babylon, and of All the Nations That Oppressed the Jews.</title> <div sID="gen18051" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10121"/><hi type="bold">1. fourth year of Jehoiakim--</hi>called the third year in <reference osisRef="Dan.1.1">Da 1:1</reference>. But probably Jehoiakim was set on the throne by Pharaoh-necho on his return from Carchemish about July, whereas Nebuchadnezzar mounted the throne January 21, 604 B.C.; so that Nebuchadnezzar's first year was partly the third, partly the fourth, of Jehoiakim's. Here first Jeremiah gives specific dates. Nebuchadnezzar had previously entered Judea in the reign of his father Nabopolassar. <div eID="gen18051" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10129"/><div sID="gen18062" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10129"/><hi type="bold">11. seventy years--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.27.7">Jr 27:7</reference>). The exact number of years of Sabbaths in four hundred ninety years, the period from Saul to the Babylonian captivity; righteous retribution for their violation of the Sabbath (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.34">Le 26:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.35">35</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.21">2Ch 36:21</reference>). The seventy years probably begin from the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when Jerusalem was first captured, and many captives, as well as the treasures of the temple, were carried away; they end with the first year of Cyrus, who, on taking Babylon, issued an edict for the restoration of the Jews (<reference osisRef="Ezra.1.1">Ezr 1:1</reference>). Daniel's seventy prophetic weeks are based on the seventy years of the captivity (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.9.2">Da 9:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">24</reference>). <div eID="gen18062" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 11. seventy years-- ( Jr 27:7 ). The exact number of years of Sabbaths in four hundred ninety years, the period from Saul to the Babylonian captivity; righteous retribution for their violation of the Sabbath ( Le 26:34 , 35 ; 2Ch 36:21 ). The seventy years probably begin from the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when Jerusalem was first captured, and many captives, as well as the treasures of the temple, were carried away; they end with the first year of Cyrus, who, on taking Babylon, issued an edict for the restoration of the Jews ( Ezr 1:1 ). Daniel's seventy prophetic weeks are based on the seventy years of the captivity (compare Da 9:2 , 24 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10130"/><div sID="gen18063" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10130"/><hi type="bold">13. all ... written in this book, which Jeremiah ... prophesied against all ... nations--</hi>It follows from this, that the prophecies against foreign nations (forty-sixth through fifty-first chapters) must have been already written. Hence the Septuagint inserts here those prophecies. But if they had followed immediately (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.13">Jr 25:13</reference>), there would have been no propriety in the observation in the verse. The very wording of the reference shows that they existed in some other part of the book, and not in the immediate context. It was in this very year, the fourth of Jehoiakim (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.1">Jr 36:1</reference>, 2), that Jeremiah was directed to write in a regular book for the first time all that he had prophesied against Judah and foreign "nations" from the beginning of his ministry. Probably, at a subsequent time, when he completed the whole work, including the forty-sixth through fifty-first chapters, Jeremiah himself inserted the clause, "all that is written in this book, which Jeremiah hath prophesied against all the nations." The prophecies in question may have been repeated, as others in Jeremiah, more than once; so in the original smaller collection they may have stood in an earlier position; and, in the fuller subsequent collection, in their later and present position. <div eID="gen18063" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10136"/><div sID="gen18074" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10136"/><hi type="bold">20. mingled people--</hi>mercenary foreign troops serving under Pharaoh-hophra in the time of Jeremiah. The employment of these foreigners provoked the native Egyptians to overthrow him. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10142"/><div sID="gen18086" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10142"/><hi type="bold">26. Sheshach--</hi>Babylon; as the parallelism in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.41">Jr 51:41</reference> proves. In the Cabalistic system (called Athbash, the first Hebrew letter in the alphabet being expressed by the last) Sheshach would exactly answer to Babel. Jeremiah may have used this system (as perhaps in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.41">Jr 51:41</reference>) for concealment at the time of this prediction, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, while Nebuchadnezzar was before Jerusalem. In <reference osisRef="Jer.51.41">Jr 51:41</reference> there can be no concealment, as Babylon is expressly mentioned. Michaelis more simply explains the term "brazen-gated" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.45.2">Is 45:2</reference>); others, "the house of a prince." Rather, it comes from the Babylonian goddess, Shach, by reduplication of the first letter; from her Misael was named Meshach by the Babylonians. The term Shace was applied to a festival at Babylon, alluded to in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.39">Jr 51:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.57">57</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.5">Is 21:5</reference>. It was during this feast that Cyrus took Babylon [Herodotus, 1]. Thus Jeremiah mystically denotes the time of its capture by this term [Glassius]. <div eID="gen18086" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10152"/><div sID="gen18107" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10152"/><hi type="bold">38. his covert--</hi>the temple, where heretofore, like a lion, as its defender, by the mere terror of His voice He warded off the foe; but now He leaves it a prey to the Gentiles [Calvin].<div eID="gen18107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18108" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fierceness of ... oppressor--</hi>rather, as the Hebrew, for "oppressor" is an adjective feminine, the word "sword" is understood, which, in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.16">Jr 46:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.16">50:16</reference>, is expressed (indeed, some manuscripts and the Septuagint read "sword" instead of "fierceness" here; probably interpolated from <reference osisRef="Jer.46.16">Jr 46:16</reference>), "the oppressing sword." The Hebrew for "oppressing" means also a "dove": there may be, therefore, a covert allusion to the Chaldean standard bearing a dove on it, in honor of Semiramis, the first queen, said in popular superstition to have been nourished by doves when exposed at birth, and at death to have been transformed into a dove. Her name may come from a root referring to the cooing of a dove. That bird was held sacred to the goddess Venus. Vulgate so translates "the anger of the dove."<div eID="gen18108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his ... anger--</hi>If the anger of Nebuchadnezzar cannot be evaded, how much less that of God (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.25.37">Jr 25:37</reference>)! <chapter eID="Jer.25"/>
